question: What are the most influential papers on VEGF angiogenesis? Return 5 with DOIs and citation counts.
final_text:
Both searches returned consistent, high-quality results. I now have all the data needed to identify the top 5 most influential papers on VEGF angiogenesis, ranked by citation count, all in the elite C1 influence class (top 0.01%).

{"answer": "The five most influential papers on VEGF angiogenesis, all classified in the top 0.01% influence tier (C1), are: (1) A landmark 2003 Nature Medicine review on the biology of VEGF and its receptors with 8,665 citations; (2) The original 1989 Science paper identifying VEGF as a secreted angiogenic mitogen with 4,925 citations; (3) A 1992 Nature paper linking hypoxia-induced VEGF to angiogenesis with 4,537 citations; (4) A 1995 Nature paper on Flk-1-deficient mice demonstrating VEGF receptor essentiality with 3,673 citations; and (5) A 1996 Nature paper on heterozygous VEGF gene knockout lethality with 3,667 citations.", "citations": [{"doi": "10.1038/nm0603-669", "title": "The biology of VEGF and its receptors", "citation_count": 8665}, {"doi": "10.1126/science.2479986", "title": "Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor Is a Secreted Angiogenic Mitogen", "citation_count": 4925}, {"doi": "10.1038/359843a0", "title": "Vascular endothelial growth factor induced by hypoxia may mediate hypoxia-initiated angiogenesis", "citation_count": 4537}, {"doi": "10.1038/376062a0", "title": "Failure of blood-island formation and vasculogenesis in Flk-1-deficient mice", "citation_count": 3673}, {"doi": "10.1038/380439a0", "title": "Heterozygous embryonic lethality induced by targeted inactivation of the VEGF gene", "citation_count": 3667}]}
